units.note: Greek says the six elephants fell 'ἅμα τοῖς ἀνδράσιν' (together with the men); English glosses this as 'their riders'. The Greek does not say whose men; left as is, ambiguous. The English lead-in 'than had been expected' is not in the Greek fragment but alters no sense.

'οὐ προγραφὰς ... ἀλλὰ καὶ προεκθέσεις' could also be read 'not only summaries but also introductions'; the rest of the chapter (προγραφαί used only in books 1-6) supports the English substitution reading.

findings.quote: because of the generals sent out from Carthage to Iberia
findings.problem: The Greek has a lacuna: 'διὰ τὸ *** τοὺς ἐπαποστελλομένους ἐκ Καρχηδόνος εἰς Ἰβηρίαν στρατηγούς'. A verb (infinitive after διὰ τὸ) is missing, so what the generals did or failed to do is lost. The English reads on as if the text were whole.
findings.proposed_fix: because [lacuna in the Greek] the generals sent out from Carthage to Iberia

findings.quote: with courage worthy of the son of Barca
findings.problem: Greek 'ἀξίως μὲν τοῦ πατρὸς Βάρκα' = worthily of his father Barca (Hamilcar). The English makes the standard the 'son of Barca', which misidentifies who is the model.

findings.quote: could no longer even remain in Italy
findings.problem: Greek 'τότε μηδ᾽ ἐν Ἰταλίᾳ νομίζειν παρεῖναι' = they thought he was not even present in Italy. The English turns this into a modal claim that he could not remain.

Greek 'ὁ δὲ' is a definite singular subject ('but he'), not 'another'. The antecedent is lost in the excerpt (likely Hannibal, the last person named), so the identity is uncertain; 'another' is unwarranted.

units.note: Antecedent of 'ὁ δὲ' is uncertain because the excerpt is a fragment; do not name Hannibal in the English.

findings.quote: but if not, they were to call the gods and the ambassadors then present from the other Greek states to witness
findings.problem: Greek has a lacuna: 'ἑτοίμως δέχεσθαι *** τοὺς θεοὺς καὶ τοὺς πρεσβευτὰς ... ἐπιμαρτυραμένους χωρίζεσθαι'. The alternative clause ('but if not') is not in the Greek; it is supplied by the translator, smoothing the gap.
findings.proposed_fix: [lacuna in the Greek] they were to call the gods and the ambassadors then present from the other Greek states to witness

findings.quote: had very nearly failed to get Attalus into his hands
findings.problem: Greek 'παρὰ μικρὸν ἔλθοι τοῦ λαβεῖν τὸν Ἄτταλον ὑποχείριον' = he came within a little of capturing Attalus (and missed him). The English 'nearly failed to get' implies he almost missed but did get him, inverting the sense of the lament.
findings.proposed_fix: had come very close to getting Attalus into his hands

findings.quote: showing bad judgment in the former case and bad temper in the latter
findings.problem: Greek 'κακῶς μὲν πρὸ τοῦ, κακῶς δὲ τότε χρώμενος τῷ θυμῷ' = using his temper badly before and badly then. The same fault (θυμός) is meant on both occasions; the English invents a contrast between judgment and temper.
findings.proposed_fix: giving way to his temper badly before and badly now

units.note: 'ὁμολογουμένως' is rendered 'by common agreement'; the sense is closer to 'undeniably', but this is not a sense error.
